PythonExport.Name: MaterialListPy

Documentation.UserDocu:
A list of materials, which behaves like a list of App.Material.
Read from a view provider it is a LIVE VIEW of that appearance: writing to it -- vp.ShapeAppearance[0].DiffuseColor = c, or one of the indexed setters below -- changes the object, records an undo step and redraws.
Assigning it anywhere else DETACHES it into a plain value. A detached list shares its storage with the one it came from until either side writes, so copying one costs nothing and mutating one never surprises the other:
a = vp.ShapeAppearance # a live view of the appearance a[0].DiffuseColor = (1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0) # changes the object
b = App.MaterialList(vp.ShapeAppearance) # a value, shares storage b[0] = mat # changes b alone vp.ShapeAppearance = b # and this is what changes the object
Indexing yields a copy of the entry with a link back, so writing a field on it writes the whole entry back to that index. The per field setters below take Index=-1 to mean every entry.
append(Material) -> None: add one entry at the end.
extend(iterable) -> None: add every material of an iterable.
insert(index, Material) -> None: insert one entry before index.

copy() -> MaterialList: a detached copy.
It shares this list's storage until one of them is written to, so it costs a pointer however long the list is.

detach() -> None: stop being a view of the object.
The list keeps the value it has and writing to it stops changing anything else. Assigning the list to a property does this too.

setSize(count, [Material]) -> None: resize the list.
Entries added take the given material, or -- with none given -- what an unset entry of this list reads as.
getMaterial(index) -> Material: one entry, as a copy.

setMaterial(index, Material) -> None: write one whole entry.
Index=-1 writes every entry.
getDiffuseColor(index) -> tuple: one entry's diffuse colour -- in PBR mode the base colour, its alpha the opacity.

setDiffuseColor([index], colour) -> None: write the diffuse colour -- in PBR mode the base colour, its alpha the opacity.
With an index it writes that entry, without one every entry.
getAmbientColor(index) -> tuple: one entry's ambient colour, which has no PBR meaning.

setAmbientColor([index], colour) -> None: write the ambient colour, which has no PBR meaning.
With an index it writes that entry, without one every entry.
getSpecularColor(index) -> tuple: one entry's specular colour -- in PBR mode the F0 tint, its alpha the metallic factor.

setSpecularColor([index], colour) -> None: write the specular colour -- in PBR mode the F0 tint, its alpha the metallic factor.
With an index it writes that entry, without one every entry.
getEmissiveColor(index) -> tuple: one entry's emissive colour.

setEmissiveColor([index], colour) -> None: write the emissive colour.
With an index it writes that entry, without one every entry.
getShininess(index) -> float: one entry's shininess -- in PBR mode the roughness.

setShininess([index], value) -> None: write the shininess -- in PBR mode the roughness.
With an index it writes that entry, without one every entry.
getTransparency(index) -> float: one entry's transparency, which is the complement of the diffuse alpha.

setTransparency([index], value) -> None: write the transparency, which is the complement of the diffuse alpha.
With an index it writes that entry, without one every entry.
getMetallic(index) -> float: one entry's metallic factor (PBR mode only).

setMetallic([index], value) -> None: write the metallic factor (PBR mode only).
With an index it writes that entry, without one every entry.
getRoughness(index) -> float: one entry's roughness (PBR mode only; in Phong mode it is derived).

setRoughness([index], value) -> None: write the roughness (PBR mode only; in Phong mode it is derived).
With an index it writes that entry, without one every entry.

insertTextureFile(path, [extension]) -> str: take a file into the store.
Answers the content hash a texture slot names it by. The store is the document's when this list is a view of one of its properties, and the process-wide one otherwise; either way the content survives being assigned into a document and is written out with it.

getTextureFile(hash) -> str: where that content is on disk.
Empty when this list does not hold it -- which a restored document does until the archive entry has been read.

getTexture(index) -> dict: one entry's maps, by slot name.
A slot the entry does not state is absent rather than empty, so `in` says what the entry says. See TextureSlots for the names.

setTexture([index], slot, hash) -> None: name content in one slot.
With an index it writes that entry, without one every entry. The hash is what insertTextureFile() answered; an empty one clears the slot.

setTextureFile([index], slot, path) -> str: insert a file and name it.
insertTextureFile() followed by setTexture(), which is what a script stating a texture from a file wants. Answers the content hash.

clearTexture([index], [slot]) -> None: unname content.
With no slot it clears every slot of the entry, and with no index it does that to every entry. Clearing the last slot of an entry clears what positioned it, because a transform with no map states nothing.
getTextureTransform(index) -> dict: Scale, Offset and Rotation.

setTextureTransform([index], Scale=, Offset=, Rotation=) -> None.
Positions the maps of an entry, or of every entry when no index is given. Scale and Offset are pairs, Rotation is in degrees. What is not named is left as it is.

clearOverrides() -> None: every face back to the base.
The whole-object write of the base is what a per-face list used to get from any uniform assignment; this is that collapse, made an action of its own.
clearOverride(index) -> None: one face back to the base.

The object's look, which every face that states nothing of its own wears.
Writing it is the whole-object write: the overriding faces keep what they hold, so an imported part with three painted faces keeps them.
The indices of the faces holding a look of their own, in order.
How many entries the list has; the same as len().
Whether writing to this list writes to the object it came from.
The texture slot names, which are also what the stored files are named by.

Whether the base is the object's material card's look, and follows it.
While it is set, assigning the object a card moves the base and the faces holding a look of their own keep it. Any whole-object write -- a colour, an appearance card, this list being assigned -- clears it. Setting it True takes the card's look at once.

Whether the stored values are read as PBR quantities.
One flag for the whole list. Setting it reinterprets the values; it converts nothing (App.Material.PBR does convert).
